title: Shakira Shuts Down Fake Endorsements in Colombian Election
summary: Shakira is not here for fake news. The Colombian superstar has forcefully denied any involvement with presidential campaigns in her home country after doctored images circulated on social media depicting her alongside candidates Iván Cepeda and Aida Quilcué. "The images circulating of me supporting presidential candidates are fake," Shakira said in a statement. "I do not support any candidate, nor have I authorized the use of my image in any campaign." The incident follows earlier unfounded rumors that she and Cepeda are distantly related. Shakira, who has largely stayed out of partisan politics, stressed her commitment to democratic principles. "My commitment is to Colombia, to its democracy and to the right of every Colombian to choose freely," she said. "My wish is for these elections to proceed transparently and in a peaceful environment for all Colombians." While she avoids endorsements, Shakira has not shied away from speaking on social issues. Last year, she reflected on the immigrant experience under the Trump administration, saying it meant "living in constant fear" and urging humane treatment regardless of policy changes. The singer moved from Colombia to the U.S. at 19 and later lived in Barcelona before settling in Miami after her split from soccer star Gerard Piqué. Currently on her Las Mujeres Ya No Lloran World Tour, Shakira performed four sold-out concerts in Colombia in February and continues this weekend in Miami Gardens. For now, her message is clear: don't believe everything you see online, and let voters make up their own minds.
why_it_matters: As deepfakes and altered images become easier to create, a fake celebrity endorsement can quickly mislead millions of voters—understanding how to spot false information is no longer optional but a crucial skill for participating in a democracy.

background_read: Shakira (full name Shakira Isabel Mebarak Ripoll) is one of the most recognizable Latin American musicians globally, known for hit songs like 'Hips Don't Lie' and for using her platform to speak on social issues such as education for underprivileged children.

Iván Cepeda is a well-known Colombian senator and human rights activist who has long campaigned for victims of the country's decades-long armed conflict; Aida Quilcué is an Indigenous Nasa leader who has sought political office and advocates for environmental and native rights.
Gerard Piqué is a Spanish football legend who played for FC Barcelona and Spain's national team; his high-profile separation from Shakira attracted massive media attention in 2022.

Colombia has a history of tight and often polarized elections, and false endorsements can sway voters—similar deepfake-like stunts have targeted celebrities in other countries, from India to the United States.

The Trump administration (2017–2021) introduced strict immigration policies, and Shakira, having lived in the U.S. since age 19, spoke out about the fear and uncertainty this created for immigrant families.

perspectives.description: By publicly calling out the manipulated images, Shakira reinforces that trustworthy information is essential for fair elections. Her intervention helps fans and voters question alarming content before sharing it, strengthening public resilience against disinformation.

When doctored visuals spread faster than the truth, even truthful campaign photos become suspect. This atmosphere of skepticism can poison political debate, making it harder to recognize genuine endorsements and ultimately harming the democratic process.

History shows that political groups have manipulated celebrity images for decades, from altered posters in the 20th century to modern AI-generated videos. This story is a fresh example of an old tactic using new technology, revealing how tech-friendly societies remain equally vulnerable to propaganda.

Moving ahead, social media platforms may adopt mandatory watermarking for AI-generated content, and schools are increasingly adding media-verification lessons. The hope is that citizens become 'pre-bunked'—trained to spot fakes before they believe them—making societies more fact-resistant.
